label: rem:extreme
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:extreme}
We adhere to Fremlin and Pryce' definition of an extreme set of a 
convex set \cite{fremlin-pryce74}, see also \cite{holmes75}. This
notion is used in Krein-Milman's theorem \cite{rudin91} and a similar 
concept appears in Bauer's maximum principle \cite{bauer58}, see 
\cite[pp.~110--113]{phelps01}. The notion of a face is rather standard
\cite{alfsen71,alfsen-shultz01,fremlin-pryce74,phelps01,rockafellar70,schneider14}.
The set $F_K(x)$ is the smallest face of $K$ that contains a given point $x\in K$ 
(in the partial order of inclusion) studied in \cite{dubins62} and 
\cite[Section~II.5]{alfsen71}, see also 
\cite{garcia-pacheco20,gorokhovik25,millan-roshchina23,weis25,weis-shirokov21}.
The definition of a face in \cite{dubins62} differs from the one presented here, 
see \cite[Section~8]{weis25} for details.
head: environment

label: pro:Alfsen
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pro:Alfsen}
For every $x\in K$ we have $F_K(x)=S_K(x)$.
head: environment
name: Alfsen

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove that $S_K(x)$ is a face of $K$, as $F_K(x)\supset S_K(x)$ 
is implied by $F_K(x)$ being an extreme set of $K$ containing $x$. Let 
$a,b,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$ satisfy $y=(1-\lambda)a+\lambda b$.
\par
 
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$S_K(x)$ is convex. If $a,b\in S_K(x)$, then there is $\epsilon>0$ such that 
$a':=x+\epsilon(x-a)$ and $b':=x+\epsilon(x-b)$ lie in $K$. Then 
$(1-\lambda)a'+\lambda b'=x+\epsilon(x-y)$ shows $y\in S_K(x)$.
 
\item
$S_K(x)$ is an extreme set. If $y\in S_K(x)$, then there is $\epsilon>0$ 
such that $y':=x+\epsilon(x-y)$ lies in $K$. Let
$\lambda_a:=\epsilon \lambda/(1+\epsilon \lambda)$ and 
$\epsilon_a:=\epsilon(1-\lambda)/(1+\epsilon \lambda)$. Then 
$(1-\lambda_a)y'+\lambda_a b=x+\epsilon_a(x-a)$ shows $a\in S_K(x)$. 
Similarly $b\in S_K(x)$. 
\qedhere
\end{itemize}

title: Definition

name: Dubins

label: remark:internal-points
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark:internal-points}
Definition~\ref{def:internal-point} replicates Dubins' concept of an ``internal 
point'' \cite{dubins62}, which we distinguish with the prefix ``D-'' here. 
Bourbaki's \emph{internal point} with respect to an affine space $A\supset K$
refers to a point $x\in K$ such that for every $a\neq x$ in $A$ there exists  
$\epsilon>0$ for which the open line segment 
$\{(1-\lambda)x+\lambda a: |\lambda|<\epsilon\}$ is included in $K$, see 
Section II.4.2 in \cite{bourbaki87}. 
\begin{itemize}
\item    
Internal points with respect to $V$ are simply called \emph{internal points} 
\cite{aliprantis-border06,bourbaki87,dunford-schwartz88,royden-fitzpatrick10}. 
They are the points $x\in K$ for which $K-x$ is \emph{absorbing} 
\cite{aliprantis-border06,bourbaki87,rudin91}. The set of internal points of 
$K$ is the \emph{core} or \emph{algebraic interior} 
\cite{barvinok02,holmes75,khazayel-etal21,zalinescu99} of $K$. 
 
\item 
The set of internal points of $K$ with respect to $\operatorname{aff} K$ is the 
\emph{intrinsic core} \cite{holmes75,khazayel-etal21,zalinescu99}
or \emph{relative algebraic interior} 
\cite{khazayel-etal21,weis-shirokov21,weis25,zalinescu99} of $K$. Clearly, the
intrinsic core of $K$ is included in the set of D-internal points  of $K$. The 
converse inclusion has been proven by Mill{\'a}n and Roshchina in 
\cite{millan-roshchina23}, Proposition 3.10, and independently in \cite{weis25}, 
Proposition~4.4. 
\end{itemize}
 
It is well known that the core 
 
\footnote{The intrinsic core of $K$ is the interior of $K$ in the relative topology of 
$\operatorname{aff} K$ induced by the finest locally convex topology on $V$\!, assuming Zermelo-Fraenkel 
set theory and the axiom of choice \cite[Section~3]{weis25}. If $\dim(K)<\infty$ then 
the intrinsic core of $K$ is known as the relative interior of $K$, which is nonempty if 
$K$ is so \cite[Section~6]{rockafellar70}.}
 
of $K$ is the interior of $K$ in the finest locally convex topology \cite[II.26]{bourbaki87} 
on $V$. The core of $K$ can be empty \cite{barvinok02,holmes75} even though $\operatorname{aff}(K)=V$.
head: environment

label: cor:internal
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:internal}
Every point $x\in K$ is a D-internal point of $F_K(x)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{pro:Alfsen} shows that for every $y\in F_K(x)$ there is $\epsilon>0$ such 
that $y':=x+\epsilon(x-y)$ lies in $K$. Since $F_K(x)$ is an extreme set of $K$ containing 
$x=\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}y+\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}y'$, it contains $y'$.

label: thm:ext
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ext}~
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
If $x\in\operatorname{ext} H$ then $\alpha|_{F_K(x)}$ is injective.
\item 
If $C$ is a singleton, $x\in H$, and $\alpha|_{F_K(x)}$ is injective, 
then $x\in\operatorname{ext} H$. 
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Injectivity criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Proceeding indirectly, we assume that $\alpha|_{F_K(x)}$ fails to be 
injective. Let $y,y'\in F_K(x)$ such that $y'\neq y$ and 
$\alpha(y')=\alpha(y)$. As depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:thm-char-ext}, there are 
$\epsilon,\epsilon'>0$ such that $F_K(x)$ contains the points 
$z:=x+\epsilon(x-y)$,
\[\textstyle
x':=\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}(z+\epsilon y')
=x+\frac{\epsilon}{1+\epsilon}(y'-y),
\quad\mbox{and}\quad
x'':=x+\epsilon'(x-x'),
\]
because $x$ is a D-internal point of $F_K(x)$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:internal}.
The constraint set $H$ contains $x'$ and $x''$ since 
$\alpha(x'')=\alpha(x')=\alpha(x)\in C$. The claim $x\not\in\operatorname{ext} H$ then 
follows from $x'\neq x$.
\par
 
(2) Let $x=(1-\lambda)x'+\lambda x''$ for some $x',x''\in H$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$. 
Since $F_K(x)$ is an extreme set of $K$ containing $x$, we have $x',x''\in F_K(x)$. 
As $C$ is a singleton, $\alpha(x'')=\alpha(x')$ holds, hence $x''=x'$ follows from 
the injectivity of $\alpha|_{F_K(x)}$, which proves $x\in\operatorname{ext} H$.

label: rem:x-internal-gen-x
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:x-internal-gen-x}
We believe the facial analysis of infinite-dimensional convex sets benefits a lot from
Alfsen's Proposition~\ref{pro:Alfsen} and its Corollary~\ref{cor:internal}, whose simple 
and intuitive use is demonstrated in \cite{weis25} and in the present paper, especially
Theorem~\ref{thm:ext}. Corollary~\ref{cor:internal} has already been stated in 
\cite[Proposition~2.3 (5)]{garcia-pacheco20} and used in 
\cite[Corollary~3.6]{millan-roshchina23}, without proofs. 
Corollary~\ref{cor:internal} and the equivalent, \emph{a priori} stronger assertion that 
every $x\in K$ lies in the relative algebraic interior of $F_K(x)$ are proved in 
\cite[Section~4]{weis25}, and, in a more complicated way, in 
\cite[Theorem 2.3]{weis-shirokov21}.

Then every point in $\operatorname{co} A$ is a convex combination of $k+1$ or fewer

title: Definition

label: pro:ext-fin
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Weizs\"{a}cker-Winkler

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) Let $x\in\operatorname{ext} H$ and $F:=F_K(x)$. Then $\dim F\leq d$ as $\alpha|_F$ is injective by 
Theorem~\ref{thm:ext}~(1). Since $F$ is a face of $K$, we have $F=K\cap\operatorname{aff} F$. As $K$ is 
linearly compact and $\dim\operatorname{aff} F<\infty$, this implies that $F$ is compact
\cite[Section~4]{kendall62}. Thus, $x\in\operatorname{co}\operatorname{ext} F$ by Minkowski's theorem, so $x$ is 
a convex combination of at most $d+1$ affinely independent extreme points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ 
of $F$ by Carath{\'e}odory's theorem. The points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ lie in $\operatorname{ext} K$, as $F$ is 
a face of $K$. Since $\alpha|_F$ is injective, the points $\alpha(x_1),\dots,\alpha(x_k)$ 
are affinely independent.
\par
 
(2) Let $x\in H'$. Then $x$ is a convex combination of at most $d+1$ extreme points 
$x_1,\dots,x_k$ of $K$. The affine independence of $\alpha(x_1),\dots,\alpha(x_k)$ implies 
that $\alpha$ restricted to $F:=\operatorname{co}\{x_1,\dots,x_k\}$ is injective. Since $F$ is a face 
of the $(d+1)$-neighborly set $K$ we have $F_K(x)\subset F$. Thus $\alpha$ restricted to 
$F_K(x)$ is injective, so Theorem~\ref{thm:ext} (2) proves the claim.
head: environment

label: exa:counter
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:counter}~
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The inclusion $\operatorname{ext} H\subset H'$ can fail if $K$ is not linearly compact.
An example is the open unit segment $K:=(0,1)$, the embedding 
$\alpha\colon K\to\mathbb{R}$, and $C:=\{\frac{1}{2}\}$.
 
\item 
All assumptions of Proposition~\ref{pro:ext-fin}~(2) are necessary 
for the inclusion $H'\subset\operatorname{ext} H$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
If $K\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is a quadrilateral, $\alpha\colon K\to\mathbb{R}$, $(x,y)\mapsto x$,
and $C:=\{x_0\}$ for some $x_0\in\alpha(K)$, then $H=\alpha^{-1}(\{x_0\})$ is 
a segment (possibly degenerated to a point) and $H'$ is the intersection of 
$H$ and the union of all non-vertical edges and diagonals of $K$. Thus, $H'$ 
is typically a set of three or four mutually distinct points of which only two 
are in $\operatorname{ext} H$. (Quadrilaterals are not two-neighborly.)
\item
If $K$ is a triangle in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\alpha\colon K\to\mathbb{R}$, $(x,y)\mapsto x$,
then, again, $H'$ is the intersection of $H$ and the union of the non-vertical edges 
of $K$. Unlike a quadrilateral, the triangle $K$ is two-neighborly. Still, 
$H'\subset\operatorname{ext} H$ fails whenever $C\cap\alpha(K)$ is more than just a point
(the assumption that $C$ is a singleton is violated).
\item 
Let $K$ be a compact convex set in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and let $\alpha\colon K\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be the 
embedding. Minkowski's and Carath\'{e}odory's theorems show $H'=H=C\cap K$. Thus, 
$H'\subset\operatorname{ext} H$ fails unless $C\cap K$ in a point or empty.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

label: rem:background-WWext
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:background-WWext}
We collect conditions for a point $x\in H$ to be an extreme point of $H$. 
For every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $H''(k)$ be the set of all points in $H$ that  
are convex combinations of at most $k$ extreme points of $K$. Dubins 
\cite{dubins62} establishes the necessity of $x\in H''(d+1)$ for linearly 
compact $K$. More generally, if the smallest face $F_H(x)$ of 
$H$ containing $x$ has dimension $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, then Klee \cite{klee63-dubins} 
shows $x\in H''(d+k+1)$. Weizs\"{a}cker and Winkler recognize the meaning 
of affine independence \cite[lemma on p.~136]{weizsaecker-winkler80} and 
\cite[Proposition~2.1]{winkler88}. They prove that $x\in H'$ is necessary 
for linearly compact $K$ and sufficient for singletons $C$ and 
$(d+1)$-neighborly $K$.

name: Summary

label: lem:basic-convexity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:basic-convexity}~
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The convex hull of every set of extreme points of a simplex is a face of 
this simplex. In particular, every simplex is $k$-neighborly for every 
$k\in\mathbb{N}$. 
\item 
Every simplex is linearly compact.
\item
Every face $F$ of $K$ inherits certain properties from $K$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
If $K$ is a simplex then so is $F$.
\item 
If $K$ is $k$-neighborly for some $k\in\mathbb{N}$ then so is $F$.
\item 
If $K$ is linearly compact then so is $F$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $(X,\mathcal{F})$ be a measurable space whose $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ contains all 
singletons in $X$. A \emph{measure} is a countably additive map $\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty)$. 
A measure $\mu$ is \emph{concentrated} on $A\in\mathcal{F}$ if $\mu(X\setminus A)=0$.
A measure $\mu$ is a \emph{probability measure} if its total mass is $\mu(X)=1$. 
Let $P$ be the convex set of probability measures on $(X,\mathcal{F})$. The 
\emph{point measure} at $x\in X$, denoted $\delta_x$, is the measure with values 
$\delta_x(A):=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A):=0$ otherwise for every $A\in\mathcal{F}$. 
Let 
\[
P_1:=\{\delta_x: x\in X\}.
\]
A measure $\mu$ is \emph{$k$-atomic} \cite{klerk-laurent19,lasserre10,nie23,schmuedgen17}, 
$k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, if $\mu=\lambda_1\delta_{x_1}+\dots+\lambda_k\delta_{x_k}$ for mutually 
distinct points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ in $X$ and strictly positive real weights 
$\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k>0$. A measure is \emph{finitely atomic} if it is $k$-atomic 
for some $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$. Let
\[
P\!_\mathrm{fin}:=
\{\mu\in P : \text{$\mu$ is finitely atomic}\,\}.
\]
head: environment

label: rem:measures-basics
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:measures-basics}
We recall basic convex geometry of the convex set $P$ of probability measures.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
A classical result by Yosida and Hewitt states that $P$ is a simplex 
\cite[Theorem~1.14]{yosida-hewitt52}, see also \cite[Section~10.11]{aliprantis-border06}. 
Thus, we refer to $P$ as the \emph{probability simplex}. There are various nonequivalent 
definitions of simplices in infinite dimensions \cite[Section~1.5]{winkler85}. The one 
using barycenters of boundary measures is much more subtle than the order theoretic one 
(of Definition~\ref{def:simplex}) we are using in this paper.
 
\item 
It is well known that a measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{F}$ is an extreme point of $P$ if and 
only if $\mu$ is two-valued. This is easy to prove using conditional probability 
measures. In particular, $P_1\subset\operatorname{ext} P$ holds. Thereby, $\mu$ is \emph{two-valued} 
if $\mu(A)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $A\in\mathcal{F}$. 
 
\item
The set $P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ of finitely atomic measures has the extreme point set $\operatorname{ext} P\!_\mathrm{fin}=P_1$ 
and $P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ is a face of the probability simplex $P$. In particular, $P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ is a 
linearly compact, $k$-neighborly simplex for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Indeed, having in mind 
$P\!_\mathrm{fin}=\operatorname{co} P_1$, one gets $\operatorname{ext} P_\mathrm{fin}\subset P_1$. In addition, $P_1\subset\operatorname{ext} P$ 
holds by (2), hence $\operatorname{ext} P_\mathrm{fin}=P_1$ and it follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:basic-convexity}~(1) 
that $P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ is a face of $P$, since $P$ is a simplex by (1). The rest follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:basic-convexity}. (More elementary proofs are possible.)
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: rem:co-countable
title: Example
body_md:
\label{rem:co-countable}
By Remark~\ref{rem:measures-basics}~(2), every point measure is an extreme 
point of $P$. The \emph{co-countable $\sigma$-algebra} 
$\{A\subset\mathbb{R}:\text{$A$ or its complement is at most countable}\,\}$
admits extreme points of $P$ that are no point measures. An example is the 
measure that assigns the value $0$ to the at most countable sets and $1$ 
to the uncountable sets \cite[Section~6.9]{schilling-kuehn21}.
head: environment
name: Co-countable $\sigma$-algebra

label: def:moment-constraints
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:moment-constraints}
Let $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}$ and let
\begin{align*}
P\!_\mathrm{a.i.}  & \textstyle 
:=\{ \mu\in P\!_\mathrm{fin} : 
\text{$\mu$ is concentrated on a finite subset $\{x_1,\dots,x_k\}\subset X$}\\
& \textstyle \hspace{\widthof{$:=\{$}}
\text{such that $\mathbf{p}(x_1),\dots,\mathbf{p}(x_k)$ are affinely independent}\,\}.
\end{align*}
We refer to the measures in $P\!_\mathrm{a.i.}$ as finitely atomic measures having the 
affine independence property. Let $C\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a  convex subset and let
\begin{align*}
G_\mathrm{fin}(C) & \textstyle
:= \{\mu\in P\!_\mathrm{fin} : \int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu\in C\},\\
 
G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C) & \textstyle
:= \{\mu\in P\!_\mathrm{a.i.} : \int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu\in C\}.
\end{align*}
Let $Q\subset P$ be a convex set of probability measures. Denoting the components of 
$\mathbf{p}=(p_1,\ldots,p_d)$ by $p_i\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$, $i=1,\ldots,d$, we define
\begin{align*}
Q^\mathbf{p} & \textstyle 
:= \{\mu\in Q : \text{$p_i$ is $\mu$-integrable $\forall i=1,\dots,d$}\,\},\\
 
G(C) & \textstyle
:= \{\mu\in Q^\mathbf{p} : \int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu\in C\}.
\end{align*}
We abbreviate $G_\mathrm{fin}(\mathbf{q}):=G_\mathrm{fin}(\{\mathbf{q}\})$, etc., for singletons 
$\{\mathbf{q}\}$ with elements $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$.
head: environment
name: Moment constraints

label: thm:moment-char-ext
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:moment-char-ext}
Consider the following assertions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The convex set $Q$ is a face of $P$. 
Furthermore, we have $\operatorname{ext} Q\subset P_1$ or $\operatorname{ext} P=P_1$.
\item 
The convex set $Q$ is a simplex and $\operatorname{ext} Q\subset P_1$.
\item 
The convex set $Q$ is linearly compact and $\operatorname{ext} Q\subset P_1$.
\item 
We have $\operatorname{ext} G(C)\subset G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then: (1)$\Rightarrow$(2)$\Rightarrow$(3)$\Rightarrow$(4).
head: environment
name: Necessary condition

title: Proof
body_md:
(1)$\Rightarrow$(2). 
Since $Q$ is a face of $P$, we have $\operatorname{ext} Q\subset\operatorname{ext} P$. So $\operatorname{ext} P=P_1$
implies $\operatorname{ext} Q\subset P_1$. Since $P$ is a simplex, its face $Q$ is also 
a simplex, see Remark~\ref{rem:measures-basics}~(1) and 
Lemma~\ref{lem:basic-convexity}~(3a).
\par
 
(2)$\Rightarrow$(3).
Every simplex is linearly compact by Lemma~\ref{lem:basic-convexity}~(2). 
\par
 
(3)$\Rightarrow$(4).
It is easy to see that $P^\mathbf{p}$ is a face of $P$. Hence, $Q^\mathbf{p}$ is a face 
of $Q$. This has two consequences. First, $Q^\mathbf{p}$ is linearly compact and 
secondly, $\operatorname{ext}[Q^\mathbf{p}]\subset\operatorname{ext} Q\subset P_1$. The claim follows then from 
Proposition~\ref{pro:ext-fin}~(1) when $K:=Q^\mathbf{p}$ and 
$\alpha\colon Q^\mathbf{p}\to\mathbb{R}^d$, $\mu\mapsto\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu$.
head: environment

label: thm:moment-char-fin
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:moment-char-fin}~
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
If $C$ is a singleton, then $G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\cap Q\subset\operatorname{ext} G(C)$.
\item
If $C$ is a singleton and $P_1\subset Q$, then $G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\subset\operatorname{ext} G(C)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Sufficient condition

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) First, $G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\subset\operatorname{ext} G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ follows from 
Proposition~\ref{pro:ext-fin}~(2) applied to $K:=P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ and 
$\alpha\colon P\!_\mathrm{fin}\to\mathbb{R}^d$, $\mu\mapsto\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu$, because 
$\operatorname{ext} P\!_\mathrm{fin}=P_1$ and because $P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ is $(d+1)$-neighborly by
Remark~\ref{rem:measures-basics}~(3). Secondly, as $P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ is a 
face of $P$, the set 
\[
P\!_\mathrm{fin}\cap Q = P\!_\mathrm{fin}\cap Q^\mathbf{p}
\]
is a face of $Q^\mathbf{p}$. Hence $G_\mathrm{fin}(C)\cap Q$ is a face of $G(C)$
as it follows from imposing the affine constraints. Combining the two, 
we have
\[
G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\cap Q
\subset 
\operatorname{ext}[G_\mathrm{fin}(C)]\cap Q
\subset
\operatorname{ext}[G_\mathrm{fin}(C)\cap Q]
\subset
\operatorname{ext} G(C).
\]
Part~(2) is a corollary of part~(1) as 
$P_1\subset Q$ implies $G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\subset Q$.
head: environment

label: cor:fin-atomic-ext
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:fin-atomic-ext}~
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The constrained set $G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ is a face of $G(C)$ if $P_1\subset Q$.
\item
We have $\operatorname{ext} G_\mathrm{fin}(C)\subset G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$.
\item
We have $\operatorname{ext} G_\mathrm{fin}(C)=G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$ if $C$ is a singleton.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Finitely atomic measures

title: Proof
body_md:
Part~(1) is revealed in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-fin}. 
Part~(2) and~(3) follow from Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-ext}~(3) and 
Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-fin}~(2) when $Q=P_\mathrm{fin}$ by 
Remark~\ref{rem:measures-basics}~(3).

label: def:Borel
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:Borel}
The \emph{$\sigma$-algebra generated by} a family of subsets of $X$ is the smallest 
$\sigma$-algebra on $X$ that includes this family. A $\sigma$-algebra on $X$ is 
\emph{countably generated} if it is generated by a countable family of subsets of 
$X$. We assume topological spaces to be Hausdorff. The \emph{Borel $\sigma$-algebra} 
on a topological space $X$, denoted by $\mathcal{B}(X)$, is the $\sigma$-algebra generated 
by the open sets. Its elements are \emph{Borel sets} and the measures on $\mathcal{B}(X)$ 
are \emph{Borel measures}.
head: environment

label: rem:two-valued
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:two-valued}
A measure $\mu\in P$ is two-valued if and only if $\mu$ is an extreme point of $P$ by
Remark~\ref{rem:measures-basics}~(2). Hence, $\operatorname{ext} P=P_1$ holds if and only if every 
two-valued probability measure on $\mathcal{F}$ is a point measure. This is true if
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$\mathcal{F}$ is countably generated \cite[p.~14]{bhaskara-rao-rao81}, see also 
\cite[Section~6.10]{schilling-kuehn21}. For example, the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(X)$ 
is countably generated if $X$ is
\begin{enumerate}
\item
a separable metric space \cite[Theorem~11 in Chapter~4]{kelley75}.
\item
a Souslin space 
 
\footnote{A \emph{Polish space} is a topological space homeomorphic to 
a complete separable metric space. A \emph{Souslin space} is a Hausdorff 
space that is the image of a Polish space under a continuous map. Every 
Borel set in a Souslin space is itself a Souslin space 
\cite[p.~96]{schwartz73}. For example, every Borel set in the 
Polish space $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a Souslin space.}
 
\cite[p.~108]{schwartz73}. 
\end{enumerate}
 
\item
$\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{B}(X)$ for a metric space $X$ of the cardinality of the continuum 
\cite{marczewski-sikorski48}. An example is the nonseparable Banach space 
$X=\ell^\infty$ of bounded real sequences (see \cite{jech03}, Chapter~3).
\end{enumerate}
See \cite{winkler88}, Example~2.1, for further spaces of probability measures 
with extreme point set $P_1$.

name: On $\ext P=P_1$

title: Example
body_md:
The measure in Example~\ref{rem:co-countable} is a Borel measure for the topology on $\mathbb{R}$ 
whose closed sets are at most countable. This topology is not Hausdorff. But there are even 
compact Hausdorff spaces that admit two-valued Borel measures that are no point measures. 
An example is the \emph{Dieudonn\'{e} measure} \cite[Example~7.1.3]{bogachev07-vol2}.

name: Borel $\sigma$-algebras with $\ext P\neq P_1$

label: pro:face-crit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pro:face-crit}
Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a set of pairs $((A_i)_{i\in I},A)$ where $(A_i)_{i\in I}\subset\mathcal{F}$ 
is an increasing net upper bounded by $A\in\mathcal{F}$ (the directed set $I$ can 
depend on the pair). Then the set of probability measures $\mu\in P$ that satisfy 
$\mu(A)=\sup_{i\in I}\mu(A_i)$ for all $((A_i)_{i\in I},A)\in\mathcal{N}$ is a face of $P$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mu,\eta,\xi\in P$, $\lambda\in(0,1)$, and $\mu=(1-\lambda)\eta+\lambda\xi$. 
Let $((A_i)_{i\in I},A)\in\mathcal{N}$. Since $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ is an increasing net, we
have
\[\textstyle
\sup_{i\in I}\mu(A_i)
=(1-\lambda)\sup_{i\in I}\eta(A_i)
+\lambda\sup_{i\in I}\xi(A_i).
\]
Since $A$ is an upper bound to $(A_i)_{i\in I}$, this implies that 
$\mu(A)=\sup_{i\in I}\mu(A_i)$ is equivalent to the conjunction of 
\[\textstyle
\eta(A)=\sup_{i\in I}\eta(A_i) 
\quad\text{and}\quad 
\xi(A)=\sup_{i\in I}\xi(A_i).
\qedhere
\]

title: Definition

name: Special Borel measures

label: cor:Borel-faces
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:Borel-faces}
Let $X$ be a topological space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
The sets $R$ and $P\!_\tau$ are faces of the simplex $P$ of Borel probability measures.
They are linearly compact, $k$-neighborly simplices for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$. 
\item 
The extreme points are $\operatorname{ext} R=\operatorname{ext} P\!_\tau=P_1$ (Tops{\o}e).
\end{enumerate}
Consider moment constraints on the ambient space $Q=R$ or $Q=P\!_\tau$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(3)]
We have $\operatorname{ext} G(C)\subset G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$.
\item[(4)] 
We have $\operatorname{ext} G(C)=G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$ if $C$ is a singleton.
\item[(5)]
The constrained set $G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ of finitely atomic measures is a face of $G(C)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Radon and $\tau$-smooth measures

title: Proof
body_md:
Part~(1). That $R$ is a face of $P$ follows from Proposition~\ref{pro:face-crit} because
the compact subsets of a Borel set are directed by inclusion, as the union of two compact 
sets is compact. Regarding the $\tau$-smooth measures, we note that every net of open 
sets is upper bounded by its union, which is open, hence Borel. The remaining statements 
follow from Remark~\ref{rem:measures-basics}~(1) and Lemma~\ref{lem:basic-convexity}.
\par
 
Part~(2). Tops{\o}e \cite[Theorem~11.1]{topsoe70} has shown $\operatorname{ext} P\!_\tau=P_1$.
The set $R$ of Radon measures is a face of $P$ by (1). Hence $R$ is a face of $P_\tau$.
This shows $\operatorname{ext} R\subset P_1$, hence $\operatorname{ext} R=P_1$.
\par
 
Part~(3) follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-ext}~(1) as $Q$ is a face of 
$P$ and $\operatorname{ext} Q=P_1$, by part~(1) and~(2).
\par
 
Part~(4) is implied by part~(3) and Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-fin}~(2),
because $P_1\subset Q$ by part~(2).
\par
 
Part~(5) follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:fin-atomic-ext}~(1) as $P_1\subset Q$
by part~(2).
head: environment

label: rem:ext-moment-contribution
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ext-moment-contribution}
The extreme points of the convex set $G(C)$ defined by $d<\infty$ many moment constraints 
on a convex set $Q\subset P$ have been characterized for the simplex $Q=R$ of Radon measures 
in \cite[Proposition~5]{weizsaecker-winkler80} and more generally for simplices $Q$ with 
the extreme point set $P_1$ in \cite[Theorem~2.1]{winkler88}. 
(The set $R$ of Radon probability measures is indeed a simplex with extreme point set $P_1$ 
by Corollary~\ref{cor:Borel-faces}~(1) and~(2) above.)
\begin{enumerate}
\item
We advance the sufficient condition for points of $G(C)$ to be extreme points by proving 
that the assumption of $Q$ being a simplex is a redundant. This is achieved in 
Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-fin}, whose main idea is that the set $P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ of finitely 
atomic measures is a face of $P$.
 
\item  
Regarding the converse, necessary condition, we introduce the novel assumption that $Q$ is 
a face of $P$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-ext}. This assumption is arguably quite strong, 
even stronger than $Q$ being a simplex. Its advantage is that no further assumptions are 
needed provided $\operatorname{ext} P=P_1$ (see Remark~\ref{rem:two-valued} for examples). Important 
examples of faces are the sets $R$ and $P\!_\tau$ of Radon and $\tau$-smooth measures, which 
are faces of the simplex $P$ of Borel probability measures by Proposition~\ref{pro:face-crit} 
and Corollary~\ref{cor:Borel-faces}.
\end{enumerate}

label: rem:Karr
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:Karr}
Karr \cite{karr83} proves $\operatorname{ext} G(\mathbf{q})=G_\mathrm{a.i.}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, for the set $Q=P$ of Borel 
probability measures on a compact metric space $X$ assuming $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is continuous. 
His proof uses the idea  \cite{douglas64} that $\mu\in G(\mathbf{q})$ is an extreme point if and only 
if $p_1,\dots,p_d$ and the constant map $X\to\mathbb{R}$, $x\mapsto 1$ span the Lebesgue space $L_1(\mu)$. 
Karr's result follows also from Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-ext}~(1) and 
Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-fin}~(2) as every compact metric space is a Polish space 
\cite[Theorem~32 in Chapter~6]{kelley75}, so $\operatorname{ext} P=P_1$ holds by Remark~\ref{rem:two-valued}~(1a).

title: Example
body_md:
The set $Q$ of Bernoulli distributions with uncertain outcomes is an open segment. 
In absence of constraints 
$G(C)=Q=\{(1-\lambda)\delta_0+\lambda\delta_1:0<\lambda<1\}$ holds. 
So $g_\mathrm{ext}(C)=+\infty$ whereas $g(C)=\min\{f(0),f(1)\}$ is finite if

name: No extreme points

title: Example
body_md:
The set $Q$ of Borel probability measures absolutely continuous with respect to  
Lebesgue measure on the unit interval $[0,1]$ is a face of the set $P$ of Borel 
probability measures on $[0,1]$, see for example \cite[Lemma 9.1]{weis25}. The 
convex set $Q$ has no extreme points because $\operatorname{ext} P=P_1$ by 
Remark~\ref{rem:two-valued}~(1a). Hence, in absence of constraints,
\[
g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)=\inf f<g(C)=0<g_\mathrm{ext}(C)=+\infty,
\]
if $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ is zero except on a set of Lebesgue measure zero and 
$\inf f<0$.

name: No finitely atomic measures

label: thm:WW-integral
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:WW-integral}
Let $C$ be closed and $Q=R$ be the simplex of Radon probability measures on a Hausdorff 
space $X$. If $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ are Borel measurable, 
and $f$ is bounded below by a real constant, then $g(C)=g_\mathrm{fin}(C)=g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)=g_\mathrm{ext}(C)$.
head: environment
name: Weizs\"{a}cker-Winkler

title: Proof
body_md:
The claim $g_\mathrm{ext}(C)\leq g(C)$ follows by monotone convergence from the integral 
representation for Radon probability measures \cite{weizsaecker-winkler79}. The proof is then 
completed by 
\[
g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\leq g_\mathrm{ext}(C)\leq g(C)\leq g_\mathrm{fin}(C)\leq g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C),
\]
as $\operatorname{ext} G(C)\subset G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$ holds by Corollary~\ref{cor:Borel-faces}~(3).
See Figure~\ref{fig:flowchart1}.
\par
 
In more detail, let $f_1,f_2,\dots$ be a countable family of Borel measurable functions 
$X\to\mathbb{R}$. Let $I$ be an index set, $\tilde C\subset\mathbb{R}^I$ a closed convex set, and for 
every $i\in I$ let $g_i\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous for the topology generated 
 
\footnote{ 
The topology on $X$ \emph{generated by} a family of subsets of $X$ is the coarsest 
topology for which all members of this family are open. The \emph{initial topology} of 
$f_1,f_2,\dots$ is the topology on $X$ generated by the preimages $f_j^{-1}(U)$, where 
$U$ is any open set in $\mathbb{R}$ and $j\in\mathbb{N}$.}
 
by the given topology of $X$ and the initial topology of $f_1,f_2,\dots$. To guarantee a 
certain degree of boundedness of the (possibly uncountably many) constraints $g_i$, we 
assume that for every $i\in I$ there is $j\in\mathbb{N}$ and a real constant $K>0$ such that 
$|g_i|\leq K(1+|f_j|)$ pointwise. Here, $|h|\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ is defined by $|h|(x)=|h(x)|$, 
$x\in X$, for every $h\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$. Let
\[\textstyle
\tilde H:=\{\nu\in R \mid
\text{$\forall j\in\mathbb{N}:f_j\subset L_1(\nu)$ 
and 
$(\int g_i\mathrm{d}\nu)_{i\in I}\in\tilde C$} \}
\]
and let $\Sigma(\operatorname{ext}\tilde H)$ be the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $\operatorname{ext}\tilde H$ such that 
$\operatorname{ext}\tilde H\to\mathbb{R}$, $\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ is measurable for every Borel set $B$ in $X$. Then 
Corollary~2 in \cite{weizsaecker-winkler79} shows that for every measure $\mu\in\tilde H$ 
there exists a probability measure $\Pi$ on $\Sigma(\operatorname{ext}\tilde H)$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:measure}\textstyle
\mu(B)=\int_{\operatorname{ext}\tilde H} \nu(B)\mathrm{d}\Pi(\nu),
\quad B\in\mathcal{B}(X).
\end{equation}
The generalized moment problem \eqref{eq:PM} with $Q=R$ fits into this setup when 
$I:=\{1,\dots,d\}$, $f_i:=g_i:=p_i$ for every $i\in I$, and $\tilde C:=C$. Equation 
\eqref{eq:measure} shows that for every $\mu\in G(C)$ there is a probability measure 
$\Pi$ on $\Sigma(\operatorname{ext} G(C))$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:integral}\textstyle
\int_X f\mathrm{d}\mu=\int_{\operatorname{ext} G(C)}(\int_X f\mathrm{d}\nu)\mathrm{d}\Pi(\nu)
\end{equation}
where $f=1_B$ is the indicator function of a Borel set $B\in\mathcal{B}(X)$, defined by 
$1_B(x):=\delta_x(B)$, $x\in X$. Equation \eqref{eq:integral} holds for every Borel 
measurable $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that is bounded below by a real constant, 
by monotone convergence, see for example \cite{bauer01}, Sections~11--12. Hence 
$g_\mathrm{ext}(C)\leq g(C)$ as $\mu\in G(C)$ is arbitrary and because the monotonicity of 
the integral shows
\[\textstyle
g_\mathrm{ext}(C)
=\inf_{\nu\in\operatorname{ext} G(C)}\int_X f\mathrm{d}\nu
\leq \int_{\operatorname{ext} G(C)}(\int_X f\mathrm{d}\nu)\mathrm{d}\Pi(\nu)
= \int_X f\mathrm{d}\mu.
\qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: rem:no-compactness
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:no-compactness}
The integral representation \eqref{eq:measure} is beyond standard Choquet theory \cite{phelps01} 
as it assumes no compactness of $\tilde H$. Of course, the simplex $R$ of Radon probability 
measures is compact in special cases. For example, if $X$ is a compact Hausdorff space, then 
$R$ is weakly-* compact \cite[Corollary~13 in Chapter~21]{royden-fitzpatrick10}. If, in addition, 
the constraints $p_1,\dots,p_d$ are bounded continuous functions and $C\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ is closed, 
then $\tilde H$ is weakly-* compact.
head: environment
name: Compactness

label: thm:RTR
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:RTR}
Let $C$ be closed and $P_1\subset Q$. If $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ and 
$f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ are arbitrary maps then $g_\mathrm{fin}(C)=g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$. If 
$\mathbf{p}$ and $f$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal{F}$, and $f$ is bounded below by a 
real constant, then $g(C)=g_\mathrm{fin}(C)=g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)=g_\mathrm{ext}(C)$.
head: environment

label: eq:bauer
title: Proof
body_md:
See Figure~\ref{fig:flowchart2} for a flowchart of the proof.
First, we focus on finitely atomic measures. Let $\mu\in G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ be a finitely 
atomic measure concentrated on $\{x_1,\dots,x_k\}\subset X$. Since $C$ is closed 
and the convex hull $F'$ of the point measures at $x_1,\dots,x_k$ is compact, it 
follows that the constrained set $F:=F'\cap G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ is compact. Bauer's maximum 
principle then shows that $\tilde\mu\mapsto\int f\mathrm{d}\tilde\mu$ attains a minimum on 
$F$ at an extreme point $\nu$ of $F$. Note that $\nu$ is an extreme point of 
$G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$, because $F'$ is a face of the simplex $P$ and so $F$ is a face of 
$G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bauer}\textstyle
g_{\operatorname{ext},\mathrm{fin}}(C)
:=\inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mu\in\operatorname{ext} G_\mathrm{fin}(C)\}
\leq g_\mathrm{fin}(C).
\end{equation}
The inclusion $\operatorname{ext} G_\mathrm{fin}(C)\subset G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$, proved in 
Corollary~\ref{cor:fin-atomic-ext}~(2), implies $g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\leq g_{\operatorname{ext},\mathrm{fin}}(C)$. 
Hence $g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\leq g_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ by \eqref{eq:bauer}, hence $g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)=g_\mathrm{fin}(C)$.
\par
 
Secondly, to study arbitrary measures in $P$, we assume that $\mathbf{p}$ and $f$ are 
measurable and $f$ is bounded below. Let $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mu\in G(\mathbf{q})$. Then 
$\mu\in Q$ and $\mathbf{q}=\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu$. If $c:=\int f\mathrm{d}\mu$ is finite, then the 
Richter-Tchakaloff theorem \cite[Theorem 1.24]{schmuedgen17}, \cite[Lemma~3.1]{shapiro01} 
shows that there is a finitely atomic measure $\nu\in P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ such that 
$\mathbf{q}=\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\nu$ and $c=\int f\mathrm{d}\nu$. Hence, 
\begin{align*}
g_\mathrm{fin}(\mathbf{q})
&=\textstyle  
 \inf\{\tilde c\in\mathbb{R}\mid \exists \nu\in P\!_\mathrm{fin}
 : \mathbf{q}=\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\nu, \tilde c=\int f\mathrm{d}\nu\}\\
&\leq\textstyle  
 \inf\{\tilde c\in\mathbb{R} \mid \exists \mu\in Q
 : \mathbf{q}=\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu, \tilde c=\int f\mathrm{d}\mu\}
 =g(\mathbf{q}).
\end{align*} 
The converse inequality $g_\mathrm{fin}(\mathbf{q})\geq g(\mathbf{q})$ holds, as $P_1\subset Q$ 
implies $P\!_\mathrm{fin}\subset Q$, so $g(\mathbf{q})=g_\mathrm{fin}(\mathbf{q})$. Taking the infimum 
over all points $\mathbf{q}\in C$ shows $g(C)=g_\mathrm{fin}(C)$.
\par
 
Now, the set $G_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ of finitely atomic measures is a face of $G(C)$ by 
Corollary~\ref{cor:fin-atomic-ext}~(1) because $P_1\subset Q$. This shows 
$\operatorname{ext} G_\mathrm{fin}(C)\subset\operatorname{ext} G(C)$ and $g_\mathrm{ext}(C)\leq g_{\operatorname{ext},\mathrm{fin}}(C)$. 
Hence $g_\mathrm{ext}(C)\leq g_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ by \eqref{eq:bauer}. Finally, 
\[
g_\mathrm{ext}(C)
\leq g_\mathrm{fin}(C)
= g(C)
\leq g_\mathrm{ext}(C).
\qedhere
\]
head: environment

label: rem:our-contrib-opti
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:our-contrib-opti}
Theorem~\ref{thm:WW-integral} has been proven in the corollary in 
\cite[p.~138]{weizsaecker-winkler80} and in \cite[Theorem~3.2]{winkler88}. We generalize
it in Theorem~\ref{thm:RTR} by replacing $Q=R$ with the weaker assumption that $Q$ 
includes the point measures $P_1$. The main ideas are summarized in 
Figure~\ref{fig:flowchart2}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
$g_\mathrm{fin}(C)\leq g(C)$ by the Richter-Tchakaloff theorem,
\item
$g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\leq g_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ by Bauer's theorem and the necessary
condition,
\item
$g_\mathrm{ext}(C)\leq g_\mathrm{fin}(C)$ by Bauer's theorem and facial geometry.
\end{enumerate}
It is tempting to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:RTR} using (1) and (2) while replacing (3) 
with $g_\mathrm{ext}(C)\leq g_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)$, which is implied by the sufficient condition 
$G_\mathrm{a.i.}(C)\subset\operatorname{ext} G(C)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:moment-char-fin}. However, the 
sufficient condition assumes that $C$ is a singleton. This underlines the advantage 
of the facial geometry in (3), which allows $C\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ to be an arbitrary closed 
convex set.

name: Summary

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be arbitrary maps.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
We say that $f$ is \emph{$\mathbf{p}$-convex} if $f=h\circ\mathbf{p}$ is the composition of $\mathbf{p}$ 
followed by  a convex function $h\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$.
 
\item
We define the \emph{$\mathbf{p}$-convex envelope} $\operatorname{env}_\mathbf{p} f\colon X\to[-\infty,+\infty]$
of $f$ pointwise by 
\[
\operatorname{env}_\mathbf{p} f(x) := \sup\{h(x): h\leq f, \text{$h$ is $\mathbf{p}$-convex\,}\},
\qquad x\in X.
\]
As before, inequalities of functions are understood pointwise.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: exa:polyconvexity
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:polyconvexity}
Let $X:=\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $d:=\binom{m+n}{m}-1$, and let $\mathbf{p}\colon\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be 
the map that returns all minors of an $m\times n$-matrix. Then the $\mathbf{p}$-convex functions 
are the \emph{polyconvex} functions introduced by J.\,M.~Ball \cite{ball76}. The $\mathbf{p}$-convex 
envelope of $f\colon\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is the \emph{polyconvex envelope} 
\cite{dacorogna08}, which is frequently denoted by $Pf:=\operatorname{env}_\mathbf{p} f$. 
\par 
 
Polyconvex energy densities play a central role in nonlinear elasticity because they allow 
one to impose physically meaningful assumptions while guaranteeing mathematical 
well-posedness. One aims at minimizing the stored energy $\int_{\Omega}f(\nabla y(x))\mathrm{d} x$
over admissible deformations $y\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^3$, given a reference configuration 
$\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$, an energy density $f$, and boundary conditions. For example, an 
energy-minimizing deformation exists if $f$ is polyconvex and satisfies certain growth 
conditions at infinity, see for example Section~8.4.2 \cite{dacorogna08}. A physically 
meaningful constraint is to penalize small determinants of  $\nabla y$ with a high energy density 
(and exclude negative determinants of $\nabla y$) to preserve the orientation. When $f$ is not polyconvex, its 
polyconvex envelope $Pf$ provides the closest relaxation that still respects physical 
constraints. The convex envelope is too rigid for modeling microstructure, already because 
it cannot have multiple local minima. This makes the polyconvex envelope an effective tool 
for modeling microstructure and for ensuring mathematically robust solutions in nonlinear 
elasticity \cite{ciarlet21,kruzik-roubicek19}.
head: environment
name: Polyconvexity

label: exa:Silhavy
title: Example
head: environment
name: Electro-magneto-elasticity

label: pro:Dacorogna
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pro:Dacorogna}
Let $\mathbf{p}\colon X\to\mathbb{R}^d$ and $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be arbitrary maps. The optimal 
value function $g_\mathrm{fin}\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ is convex and satisfies $g_\mathrm{a.i.}=g_\mathrm{fin}$. 
If $f$ is bounded below by a $\mathbf{p}$-convex function, then $g_\mathrm{fin}>-\infty$ pointwise and 
$\operatorname{env}_\mathbf{p} f=g_\mathrm{fin}\circ\mathbf{p}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $\mu\mapsto\int f\mathrm{d}\mu$ and $\mu\mapsto\int p_i\mathrm{d}\mu$, $i=1,\dots,d$ 
are real affine maps on the convex set 
$\tilde P\!_\mathrm{fin}:=\{\mu\in P\!_\mathrm{fin}:\int f\mathrm{d}\mu<\infty\}$. Hence, 
$\tilde g_\mathrm{fin}\colon \mathbb{R}^d\to[-\infty,+\infty]$,
\[\textstyle
\tilde g_\mathrm{fin}(\mathbf{q}):=
\inf\{\int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \mathbf{q}=\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu, \mu\in\tilde P\!_\mathrm{fin}\},
\qquad \mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d,
\]
is convex by Theorem~1 and Example~1 in \cite{rockafellar74}. And so is 
$g_\mathrm{fin}=\tilde g_\mathrm{fin}$. The equality $g_\mathrm{a.i.}=g_\mathrm{fin}$ is shown in
Theorem~\ref{thm:RTR} as the singletons $\{\mathbf{q}\}$ are closed for all
$\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$.
\par
 
Let $f$ be bounded below by a $\mathbf{p}$-convex function, say $h\circ\mathbf{p}\leq f$ and
$h\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is convex. Jensen's inequality 
\cite[Theorem~4.3]{rockafellar70} shows that for every $\mu\in P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ we have
\[\textstyle
h(\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu)
\leq \int h\circ\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu
\leq \int f\mathrm{d}\mu.
\]
Minimizing for a fixed $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ the right-hand side of $h(\mathbf{q})\leq\int f\mathrm{d}\mu$
over all $\mu\in P\!_\mathrm{fin}$ that satisfy $\mathbf{q}=\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu$, we get 
$-\infty<h\leq g_\mathrm{fin}$ pointwise. For every $x\in X$, the constraint 
$\mathbf{p}(x)=\int\mathbf{p}\mathrm{d}\mu$ is satisfied by the point measure $\mu=\delta_x$, hence
\[\textstyle
h\circ\mathbf{p}
\leq g_\mathrm{fin}\circ\mathbf{p}
\leq f.
\]
Thus, $g_\mathrm{fin}\circ\mathbf{p}$ is a $\mathbf{p}$-convex lower bound to $f$, so 
$g_\mathrm{fin}\circ\mathbf{p}\leq \operatorname{env}_\mathbf{p} f$. Maximizing for a fixed $x\in X$ the left-hand 
side of $h\circ\mathbf{p}(x)\leq g_\mathrm{fin}\circ\mathbf{p}(x)$ over all convex functions 
$h\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ that satisfy $h\circ\mathbf{p}\leq f$, we conclude 
$\operatorname{env}_\mathbf{p} f\leq g_\mathrm{fin}\circ\mathbf{p}$.

label: exa:convex-env
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:convex-env}
Let $X:=\mathbb{R}^d$ and let $\mathbf{p}\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be the identity map. Then the $\mathbf{p}$-convex 
functions are simply the convex functions $\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. The $\mathbf{p}$-convex 
envelope of $f\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is simply the \emph{convex envelope} 
\cite{dacorogna08}, which is frequently denoted by $Cf:=\operatorname{env}_\mathbf{p} f$. We have 
$C f\leq\operatorname{co} f$, where $\operatorname{co} f\colon\mathbb{R}^d\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ is the greatest convex 
function below $f$ (the \emph{convex hull} of $f$). It is well known that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:convex-hull}\textstyle
\operatorname{co} f(x)=\inf\{\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}\lambda_if(x_i) : x=\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}\lambda_ix_i\},
\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^d,
\end{equation}
where the infimum is taken over all expressions of $x$ as a convex combination of $d+1$ points. 
The formula \eqref{eq:convex-hull} is also valid if one takes only the combinations in which 
the points $x_i$ whose weights $\lambda_i$ are strictly positive are affinely independent 
\cite[Corollary~17.1.5]{rockafellar70}. If $f$ is bounded below by a convex function 
$\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, then $C f=\operatorname{co} f$ and the formula \eqref{eq:convex-hull} and its 
affine independence statement follow immediately from Proposition~\ref{pro:Dacorogna}.

label: exa:polyconvex-envelope
title: Example
body_md:
\label{exa:polyconvex-envelope}
Let $\mathbf{p}\colon\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^d$ be the minor map of Example~\ref{exa:polyconvexity}. 
Dacorogna has shown that if $f\colon\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is bounded below 
by a polyconvex function, then the polyconvex envelope of $f$ is 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:poly-envelope}\textstyle
P f(M)
=\inf\{\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}\lambda_if(M_i) : \mathbf{p}(M)=\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}\lambda_i\mathbf{p}(M_i)\},
\qquad M\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},
\end{equation}
where the infimum is taken over all tuples $(M_1,\ldots,M_{d+1})$ and 
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_{d+1})$ of $m\times n$ matrices and nonnegative real weights 
that sum to one, respectively---in other words, over all expressions of $M$ as a convex 
combination of $d+1$ matrices that satisfy additional nonlinear constraints (linear in 
the minors) \cite[Theorem~6.8]{dacorogna08}. Because of these additional constraints,
the convex envelope of Example~\ref{exa:convex-env} satisfies $C f\leq P f$. Formula
\eqref{eq:poly-envelope} reads $Pf=g_{d+1}\circ\mathbf{p}$, where 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gd1}\textstyle
g_{d+1}(\mathbf{q}):=
\inf\{ \int f\mathrm{d}\mu : \text{$\mu\in G_\mathrm{fin}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mu$ is $k$-atomic for some $k\leq d+1$}\,\},
\qquad \mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d.
\end{equation}
Since $g_\mathrm{fin}\leq g_{d+1}\leq g_\mathrm{a.i.}$ is clear, we retrieve $Pf=g_{d+1}\circ\mathbf{p}$ from 
Proposition~\ref{pro:Dacorogna} above. The expression $P f=g\circ\mathbf{p}$ of 
Corollary~\ref{cor:Dacorogna}, where $g$ is the optimal value function \eqref{eq:PM} on Borel 
measures, is also well known, see e.g.\ \cite{fantuzzi-etal26} and the references therein.
\par
 
Furthermore, Corollary~\ref{cor:Dacorogna} shows $P f=g_\mathrm{ext}\circ\mathbf{p}=g_\mathrm{a.i.}\circ\mathbf{p}$. Not 
only are the optimal value functions $g_\mathrm{ext}=g_\mathrm{a.i.}$ equal, but also the constraint sets 
$\operatorname{ext} G(\mathbf{q})=G_\mathrm{a.i.}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d$, by Corollary~\ref{cor:Borel-faces}~(4). To the
best of our knowledge, these assertions are novel, although they follow immediately from 
Weizs\"{a}cker and Winkler's Theorem~\ref{thm:WW-integral} and Dacorogna's formula 
\eqref{eq:poly-envelope}.

name: Old and new representations of the polyconvex envelope

label: rem:envelopes
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:envelopes}
We have shown that optimal value functions of generalized moment problems are generalized 
convex envelopes (Proposition~\ref{pro:Dacorogna} and Corollary~\ref{cor:Dacorogna}). We 
are unaware of literature on this topic aside from the references in 
Example~\ref{exa:convex-env} and Example~\ref{exa:polyconvex-envelope}. Regarding the 
polyconvex envelope, the representations $P f=g_\mathrm{ext}\circ\mathbf{p}=g_\mathrm{a.i.}\circ\mathbf{p}$ using optimal 
value functions on extreme points and on finitely atomic measures that have the affine 
independence property seem to be new. The representations $P f=g_{d+1}\circ\mathbf{p}=g\circ\mathbf{p}$ 
with optimal value functions on finitely atomic measures and on Borel measures are well 
known \cite{dacorogna08,fantuzzi-etal26}.
